summary: Alaska light (1903) on a reef in Clarence Strait, wrecked by storms and rebuilt on Lincoln Island. The 1903 tower is gone; a modern light still shows.

access.note: Coast Guard property, reached by boat; not open to the public.

events.note: Site reserved for lighthouse purposes by executive order, 1 July 1901.
Concrete pier and wooden house built by hired labour after the 1902 contract was annulled in June 1903.
Fourth-order fixed white light to show on or about 1 December 1903 (Notice to Mariners, as quoted by LighthouseFriends).
Storm of 28 November 1909 swept the lighthouse; keepers taken off by an Army ship (LighthouseFriends).
Storm of 4 April 1910 rolled seas into the lower floor.
Keepers evacuated the rock in December 1910 after a temporary light.
New station commissioned 10 October 1912: light on the rock; dwelling and fog signal on Lincoln Island (CoastView gives 1911).
Keeper Norval S. Douglas and assistant Gardner Tibbetts aided two men whose launch had been wrecked (2 December 1914).
A keeper's logbook entry records the USS Henderson passing with President Harding aboard on 9 July 1923 (as quoted by LighthouseFriends).
Coast Guard took over Alaska's aids to navigation.
Lighthouse personnel removed on 20 March 1968; a battery-operated light was left on the rock; the station was discontinued in 1968.
Facilities on Lincoln Island demolished; only the foundations remain.

corrections.proposed: active (modern light on a steel skeleton tower; the 1903 station is gone)
corrections.why: CoastView (2026) says a modern light is currently active on Lincoln Rock. The archive's 'Active Aid to Navigation: No' refers to the 1903 structure.
The archive gives 'Existing: No' and 'Only Foundation Remains'; CoastView says only the building foundations remain.

resolved_conflicts.explanation: CoastView dates the contract to March 1902 and the late-1903 completion; LighthouseFriends and the Douglas Island News of September 1903 describe the same build. The 1903 date stands.

CoastView gives 10 October 1911 as the completion date. The 1915 Commissioner's report gives 10 October 1912 for the station being placed in commission and says the work was completed in the 1915 fiscal year. The 1912 date is used; the CoastView date is not supported by the official report.

notes_for_editor: Unresolved: (1) Distance to Lincoln Island: LighthouseFriends says about 1,650 feet east; CoastView says about 1,300 feet (400 m) east of the rock; the Wikipedia article (lead only) says about 440 yards. The story gives both sources' figures. (2) The Army ship Paterson rescue after the 28 November 1909 storm comes from LighthouseFriends only; the Wrangell paper read gives no ship name, so the story attributes it to LighthouseFriends. (3) The 1923 logbook quotation is LighthouseFriends's transcription; the log itself was not seen. (4) The Coast Guard Historian's Lincoln Rock article is on history.uscg.mil; its archived copy was not available (the Internet Archive path returned 404), so no Coast Guard primary text for the modern light was read. (5) Current status of the modern light rests on CoastView (2026) and the Wikipedia infobox (lead only). (6) The Douglas Island News OCR reads the contractor's name as 'Carkeek'; the story leaves the name out because the OCR is not clean. (7) The Wrangell Sentinel of 22 December 1910 mentions a keeper Peterson moving to Lincoln Rock from another station; it is not tied to the roster's Carl E. Peterson, and no other_stations link is made. (8) Roster names for keepers after 1960 are in the keeper rows only; the prose does not name them. (9) The 1901 Light-House Board passage on Lincoln Rock was not used (scan page uncertain). (10) Newspapers: one Chronicling America search (Lincoln Rock, Alaska, 1903-1912) returned 50 pages; four were read. The 1909 storm and 1910 evacuation rest on the Wrangell pages and LighthouseFriends; no Wrangell page about the 1910 evacuation itself was read. (11) Scan pages for the Commissioner's report (scan 59 = printed 54; scan 70 = printed 65) are from the corpus OCR index; printed pages were marked as read there. (12) The 99 is the number of roster lines roster.py prints from the archive page; the page itself does not print a total. (13) The 1911 (CoastView) and 1912 (Commissioner's report) dates are both stated in the story, which follows the official report for commissioning. (14) The 1910 Wrangell item names no first name and is not tied to the archive's Carl E. Peterson lines; the roster line for 1910-1912 now cites only the archive.
